title: The Deep Range
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 4 of 40
content:
The transmitter was lodged inside a synth that had tried very hard to kill us.

That felt appropriate.

Danse pried the component from the ruined torso with the methodical focus of a mechanic dismantling an appliance. I stood nearby with my weapon ready, watching the corridor and trying not to stare at the black scorch marks across his armor.

The engine blast had burned away old paint. Beneath it, bare metal showed through like exposed bone.

Every time I looked at it, I remembered the moment he disappeared inside the fire.

Apparently my face was not subtle.

“You can stop checking,” he said.

“I’m watching the hallway.”

“You’ve looked at my armor six times in the last minute.”

“You counted?”

“I notice patterns.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

“It keeps me alive.”

He freed the transmitter and placed it in a hard case.

“So does power armor, evidently.”

He looked at me.

“You’re still angry.”

“No.”

“You are.”

“I’m thrilled. I love activating rocket engines under people I met an hour ago.”

“That was a tactical decision.”

“It was a terrible tactical decision.”

“It worked.”

“That does not retroactively make it smart.”

His jaw shifted.

For a moment I expected another order.

Instead he said, “Fair.”

I blinked.

“What?”

“You had incomplete information. From your perspective, the risk was unreasonable.”

“You’re apologizing.”

“I’m acknowledging your concern.”

“That is the most militarized apology I’ve ever received.”

“It wasn’t an apology.”

“Of course not.”

We took the elevator back toward the surface.

The ride was close and loud. Danse’s armor occupied most of the small compartment. I stood beside him with my shoulder nearly against one metal elbow while ancient cables groaned above us.

The silence felt different now.

Before the engine room, I had known him as a competent stranger with a command problem.

Now I knew what his face looked like after surviving something that should have killed him.

That seemed dangerously personal.

He broke the silence first.

“You did well in there.”

“Is this where I get the sticker?”

“No.”

“Shame.”

“I’m serious.”

The elevator rattled.

Danse looked straight ahead.

“You followed instructions under pressure. You adapted when circumstances changed. You covered my flank without needing to be told.”

“I also argued with you repeatedly.”

“That part needs work.”

I smiled.

“There he is.”

His eyes flicked toward me.

“Who?”

“The man who cannot deliver a compliment without attaching corrective feedback.”

“That’s how people improve.”

“Have you ever considered just saying something nice and then stopping?”

He actually seemed to think about it.

“No.”

The elevator doors opened.

We stepped into daylight that looked too gentle for what had happened underground.

Outside ArcJet, Danse finally removed his helmet and took a long breath of cold air.

I leaned against a concrete barrier.

“What now?”

“We return to Cambridge. Haylen should be able to use the transmitter to boost our signal.”

“And then?”

“If we establish contact, command decides our next move.”

“You sound excited.”

“I am.”

That surprised me.

He noticed.

“The Brotherhood is more than an organization,” he said. “For some of us, it’s the closest thing we have to a home.”

There was no performance in his voice this time. No recruitment speech.

I studied him.

“You’ve been out here a long time.”

“Long enough.”

“With people dying.”

His expression closed immediately.

I regretted it.

“I saw the list,” I said.

Danse looked toward the road.

“Four members of my squad are dead.”

No names. No details.

But the words were heavy.

“I’m sorry.”

“So am I.”

There was something terrible about the simplicity of that answer.

He resealed the helmet.

“We should move.”

The subject was over.

I let it be.

Halfway back to Cambridge we found a trader pinned behind a delivery truck by raiders. Danse spotted the muzzle flashes first.

“Two on the roof. One behind the blue sedan.”

“You want to get involved?”

“They’re attacking a civilian.”

That was apparently sufficient explanation.

He went left. I went right.

The fight lasted less than a minute.

Afterward, the trader crawled from cover with both hands raised.

“I don’t have much,” she said quickly. “Take whatever. Just—thanks.”

Danse lowered his rifle.

“We’re not robbing you.”

She stared at the Brotherhood symbol on his armor.

“I heard things.”

“I’m sure you have.”

His tone cooled, but not at her.

He looked at the damaged wheel on her cart.

“Axle’s bent.”

“I know.”

“You’ll lose the wheel before you reach Diamond City.”

“I know.”

Danse set his rifle against the truck and crouched.

I watched in amazement as he pulled a compact toolkit from a storage compartment on his armor.

“What?” he asked without looking up.

“You carry tools.”

“Everyone should carry tools.”

“That might be the first thing we completely agree on.”

He grunted.

Together we braced the axle well enough to get the trader moving. She tried to pay us again. Danse refused.

When she was gone, I crossed my arms.

“Brotherhood policy?”

“Basic decency.”

“Careful. You’re ruining your image.”

“What image?”

“Terrifying machine in terrifying machine.”

He turned his helmet toward me.

“I’m not a machine.”

The response was immediate. Sharper than the joke deserved.

I raised my hands.

“Figure of speech.”

He looked away.

“Right.”

The moment passed.

At the time, I thought nothing of it.

Later, I would remember it with painful clarity.

Back at Cambridge, Haylen nearly hugged the transmitter case.

Rhys looked at me as though disappointed I had survived.

Danse disappeared into the garage and returned carrying a laser rifle.

He held it out to me.

I stared at the weapon.

“What’s this?”

“Payment.”

“That is worth more than the caps you offered.”

“Yes.”

The rifle was beautifully maintained. Custom optics. Modified internals. The kind of weapon someone cared for, not merely used.

I looked up.

“This was yours.”

“It was.”

“You’re giving me your rifle?”

“I have another.”

“That is not the point.”

Danse’s expression tightened with the particular discomfort he seemed to experience whenever a conversation threatened to become personal.

“You earned it.”

I took the rifle.

Our hands did not touch. He was still wearing gloves.

Still, something about the exchange felt intimate.

“Does it have a name?” I asked.

“Righteous Authority.”

I stared at him.

He stared back.

“You named your gun Righteous Authority.”

“I didn’t ask for commentary.”

“Oh, you’re getting commentary.”

Haylen laughed from across the room.

Danse closed his eyes briefly.

For the first time since meeting him, I realized I had found a weapon more effective than a laser rifle.

I could embarrass Paladin Danse.

That knowledge was going to be dangerous.

The trip back to Cambridge should have been easier.

We had what we came for. The signal booster sat wrapped in cloth inside my pack, ArcJet burned behind us, and the road was familiar enough that Danse relaxed his pace by a fraction.

Then rain started.

Not clean rain. Commonwealth rain that smelled faintly metallic and made both of us check our dosimeters before deciding it was ordinary misery rather than radioactive misery.

We took shelter beneath the remains of a Red Rocket canopy.

Danse stepped out of his armor to clear grit from the damaged knee actuator. Without the suit he seemed simultaneously larger and more human—broad shoulders, fatigues dark with sweat, movements missing the hydraulic certainty I had already begun associating with him.

“You’re limping,” I said.

“I am not.”

“You absolutely are.”

“The suit was compensating for uneven ground.”

“You are currently not wearing the suit.”

He looked down at his own leg as if betrayed by evidence.

“Minor strain.”

“Sit.”

His head came up.

“That was an order,” I added.

“You are not authorized to issue me orders.”

“Partnership. Remember?”

He stared at me long enough that I expected a lecture.

Instead he sat on an overturned bucket.

I crouched and checked the knee through his fatigues. No swelling worth panicking over, but the muscle was tight.

“Probably from compensating for the actuator.”

“I’m aware.”

“Then why didn’t you fix it?”

“The mission took priority.”

“Your leg came with us on the mission.”

Danse opened his mouth.

Closed it.

“That is an irritatingly valid point.”

“I have those occasionally.”

I found a strip of clean cloth and wrapped the joint enough to support it until we returned.

He watched my hands.

“You’ve done field medicine.”

“I’ve done Commonwealth medicine. Mostly that means deciding whether something needs a bandage, a stimpak, or a very convincing lie.”

“What does the lie treat?”

“Panic.”

He considered that with surprising seriousness.

“Morale management.”

“Sure. We’ll call it that.”

Rain hammered the rusted canopy.

For a few minutes there was nowhere useful to go and nothing trying to kill us. Danse seemed almost uncomfortable with the absence of a task.

His gaze tracked the road anyway.

“You never stop, do you?” I asked.

“Stop what?”

“Being on watch.”

“Someone should be.”

“Even when someone else is?”

His eyes shifted to me.

I had meant myself.

He understood.

The next answer took longer.

“Habit.”

It was becoming one of his words. A place he stored explanations he did not want to unpack.

I leaned back against a support pillar and looked out at the rain.

“Well. For five minutes, I’m on watch.”

“That’s unnecessary.”

“Probably.”

He frowned.

Then, with visible effort, he let his shoulders drop against the wall behind him.

Not much.

Enough.

When the rain eased, he stood and climbed back into the armor.

The left knee moved smoothly after I cleaned the housing.

Danse took two steps, stopped, and looked down at me.

“Your assessment was correct.”

“That sounded painful.”

“It was.”

“Want me to pretend I didn’t hear it?”

“No.”

A pause.

“Thank you.”

I had not expected that either.

By the time Cambridge came into view, I was starting to understand that Paladin Danse had more ways to surprise me than he had ways to smile.
